lessons.title: Getting ready to pack
lessons.html:
Packing is the last touch

The packer is the last person to handle the fruit before the customer opens the carton, maybe in London, Dubai or Shanghai. A well-packed carton protects the fruit, looks good and contains exactly what the label says.

Know the pack specification

Before you start, your supervisor or the pack instruction card tells you:

  • The fruit, cultivar and grade (class) being packed.
  • The size or count: how many fruit go in a carton, or the size range.
  • The carton type and any inner packaging: trays, liners, bags, wraps or punnets.
  • The pack pattern: how fruit must lie in the carton.
  • The weight the carton must reach.
  • The market and labels needed.

If you are not sure, ask before you start. A whole pallet packed wrong must be repacked.

Prepare your work station

  1. Wash your hands and put on your clean apron, hairnet and any gloves required.
  2. Remove jewellery, watches and anything that could fall into a carton.
  3. Check that your station is clean.
  4. Have enough cartons, trays, liners and labels within reach.
  5. Check that the cartons are the right type and not damaged, wet or dirty.

Check each fruit

Even after grading, check each fruit as you pick it up. Take out fruit with defects, the wrong size or the wrong colour for that grade and put it in the correct return bin. Do not pack fruit that has fallen on the floor.

Remember that a carton of export fruit can be worth several hundred rand. Careful packing protects the farm's income and your packhouse's name.

lessons.title: Packing to specification
lessons.html:
Packing the carton

  1. Place the liner, bag or tray in the carton as shown on the instruction card.
  2. Pick fruit up gently with your whole hand. Do not squeeze, drop or throw it.
  3. Place the fruit in the correct pattern, for example with stems all facing the same way, or in a set number of rows. Tray packs have one fruit per cup.
  4. Pack firmly so fruit does not move and rub during transport, but do not press fruit in so tightly that it bruises.
  5. The fruit must not stick up above the carton edge, or the lid will crush it.
  6. Fold or close the liner if one is used.

Count and weight

Each carton must have the right count or weight. Many packhouses check-weigh cartons on a scale. If a carton is underweight, add fruit of the same size; if it is over, take fruit out. Do not over-pack to be safe; giving away extra fruit costs the farm money and can break the size rules.

Labelling and traceability

Every carton is marked with information such as the packhouse code, the producer or orchard code, the packing date, the cultivar, class and count. This is called traceability: if there is a problem in the market, the carton can be traced back to where it came from. Put labels and stickers exactly where the instruction says, straight and clean. Some packhouses also record a packer number on each carton.

Common faults to avoid

FaultResult
Loose packFruit moves and bruises
Over-tight packPressure bruising, lid damage
Mixed sizes or coloursCarton fails inspection
Wrong or missing labelPallet may be rejected

Inspection

Quality controllers and sometimes government inspectors check cartons. If your cartons are rejected, listen to the reason and correct it.

Key points

  • Follow the pack specification: grade, count, carton, pattern, weight and market.
  • Prepare a clean station and check cartons before packing.
  • Handle fruit gently and pack firmly in the correct pattern.
  • Make sure count or weight is correct.
  • Label every carton correctly for traceability.
